runs.text: preßa a fugir decà pera là.

lines.note: Continues the preceding page's description of settlements taking hurried flight, scattering here and there. Preßa is running text here; its occurrence in the preceding page's lower margin is only a catchword.
Nigejini means dying while fleeing. The headword is visibly continuous, rather than the draft's Nigue jini; the following example divides the same compound at the line end.
Completes nigejini wo suru, to die in flight. Idem refers back to the headword's definition.
Nigejiri is illustrated by cutting someone from behind while fleeing, with the alternative passive kiraruru. The passive form is divided after qira-; Latin l is not part of the Japanese.

runs.text: Ferir, ou ſer ferido por de tras.

lines.note: Completes kiraruru and translates the active/passive pair as wounding or being wounded from behind. The printed de tras spacing is retained.
Nigejitaku means preparation or arrangements for flight. The Portuguese geito is retained rather than modernized to jeito.
Nigemawari means moving about in flight through different places. The physical division par-tes begins its extended Portuguese explanation.

runs.text: tes, ou furtar o corpo de muitas maneiras pera

lines.note: Completes partes and adds evading someone in many ways. The purpose of this evasive movement follows below.
The purpose is to avoid encountering someone. This closes the nigemawari gloss rather than introducing a separate reflexive verb entry.
Nigemayoi means wandering astray while fleeing. Both principal-part o marks visibly point upward, so the draft's first ǒ is corrected to ô; the Portuguese adjective continues below.
Completes desgarrado and begins an example of religious and lay people, men and women, fleeing east and west. The spelling nannho is retained rather than normalized to a modern reading.

Mayoo completes nigemayoo. The upright Taif. citation is followed by italic book 28 and the translation beginning with religious people; the citation's final stop is kept outside the italic apparatus.
The translation includes lay people as well as religious people, men as well as women, all fleeing. Homẽs retains its printed abbreviation mark.

runs.text: dos, & diſperſos ſem ſaber poronde hião.

lines.note: Completes fugidos and describes them as scattered, not knowing where they were going. The close-set poronde and historical hião remain unchanged.
Nigen, alternatively nigon, is explained as futatsu no kotoba, two utterances. The Portuguese definition continues below and connects the term with repeating one's words.

runs.text: palauras, ou o repetir de palaura. ¶

lines.note: The gloss gives two words or repetition of an utterance. Cũ- begins kunshi in the example below; the tilde abbreviates the nasal and the entire Japanese fragment is upright, not partly italic.
Kunshi ni nigen nashi says that a gentleman or wise person does not speak with two voices. The Portuguese renders the person as wise and prudent; pru continues below without an inferred hyphen.
Completes prudente and says that such a person does not have many words. This is the dictionary's paraphrase, not an editorial replacement by a more familiar modern proverb translation.
Nigenobi means getting far ahead while escaping. The two printed dictionary-form alternatives bu and uru are retained as given.

runs.text: diãte dos que vem no alcance.

lines.note: The fugitives are far ahead of those pursuing them. The contracted diãte completes the preceding muito and is not expanded in the transcription.
Nigueſari denotes withdrawing or getting away in flight; the Portuguese offers taking refuge and, on the next row, moving away. The three verb forms remain on one physical line.
Apartarſe completes the alternative definition of Nigueſari: separating oneself or withdrawing. This is a short indented continuation, not a new entry.

Nigue vxe combines flight with disappearance. The first Portuguese letter survives in a T-like form, so the aligned draft's Tugindo is retained. Fugindo is clearly intended by the sense and neighboring entries, but a worn F cannot be distinguished securely from a printed T here; the uncertainty is not silently normalized.
Nigui is equated with Tenchi, heaven and earth. The pilcrow starts a further expression whose first element is physically divided Ni-/gui across the row boundary.
Ni-/gui caifiacu is explained as dating from the creation of the world. The old Portuguese spacing Deſda and the separately printed upright S. are preserved.
Niguiniguito is labeled an adverb and describes a display or bustle of people. The tilde and terminal hyphen in gẽ- belong to the printed abbreviation and continuation.
The gloss continues with people and festivity, then introduces a Japanese example concerning the inside of a household. The roman example is physically divided at nigui-.
This completes the example's niguiniguito miyeta. The Portuguese begins describing how the interior of the house appeared; mo- continues as modo on the next row.

runs.text: do de aparato, tumulto de gente, & abaſtan

lines.note: The house presents an appearance of display, bustling people and abundance. The final abaſtan continues into ça below without a visible printed hyphen, which has not been supplied.
Ça completes abaſtança, abundance, and closes the household example. The short continuation remains a separate indented physical row.

runs.text: Couſa de concurſo de gente, a-

lines.note: Niguiniguixij describes something crowded, lively or festive. The Portuguese begins with a gathering of people and divides a-/parato across the next boundary.
Aparato and feſta complete the description with display and festivity. This is the continuation of the adjective's gloss, not a separate definition.
This indented derivative is the corresponding noun in -ſa, liveliness or festive bustle. The visible internal space is retained rather than joining it to match the main headword.
The second indented derivative gives the adverbial form in -xǔ. The opening stroke of the repeated element is worn, but the printed spacing and marked final vowel remain recoverable.
Niguiri means gripping or squeezing with the hand. The entry supplies the usual three verb forms, followed by a figurative example on the next row.
The example pictures holding the world in one's palm. Its Portuguese interpretation begins Senho-, continuing into the verb for ruling or mastering below.
Together with Senho- above, this says to rule the whole world. It completes the figurative application of gripping something in one's hand.

runs.text: Lugar por onde tomão o arco cõ a mão

lines.note: This separate noun entry denotes the grip of a bow, the place held with the hand. The nasal abbreviation cõ is retained, and the specification of which hand continues below.
The grip is held with the left hand and is covered in leather. This finishes the definition of the bow part rather than describing a different item.
Niguiricobuxi denotes a clenched fist. The Portuguese phrase Punho ſeco is followed by an example whose noun is divided Niguiri-/cobuxi across rows.
The example means striking with a fist. Depunhadas retains the source's close spacing; the alternative Portuguese wording is completed on the following row.

This repeats the clenched-fist expression. The partly abraded vowel in punho is read as u, consistent with its surviving strokes and the clearer occurrence two rows above, rather than the draft's penho.
Niguiuai is the noun for bustle or prosperity, glossed through a display of people and abundance. The faint middle letters are retained as the same stem used in the next entry.

The corresponding verb means having bustle, display and abundance. Both marked o forms show the downward-pointing accent of ǒ. Enlarged reinspection shows a point after aparato rather than a descending comma; that unusual punctuation is preserved.
Niguiyacana describes a lively or festive scene involving people and display. The printed apara- continues into apparatus or display on the next physical row.
To completes aparato and closes the adjective's Portuguese explanation. Its short length does not make it page furniture or an independent entry.
The two indented forms give the adverb in -ni and the noun in -ſa associated with Niguiyacana. They are printed together on one row without additional Portuguese glosses.
Nigura is glossed as a pack saddle. This final left-column entry stands above the bottom rule and is body text, distinct from the signature and catchword elsewhere below the page.
Nigin is paraphrased as Mimino chiri, dust of the ears. The Portuguese likewise gives dirt or dust in the ears; chiri has h rather than the draft's b, and ou- continues below.
After completing ouuidos, the entry gives a figurative example about brushing away the ears' dust and listening. The example repeats Nigin with uo; the draft's Niguiuo confuses the medial strokes.
The Portuguese interprets the figurative expression as listening attentively. The final S. is upright and separate from the italic translation.
Niji means a rainbow, literally the sky's bow in the Portuguese gloss. Nijiga tatçu introduces its appearance or formation, with Fazer- continued on the next row.
The first phrase finishes the rainbow's formation; the second describes its disappearance. Both the intervening pilcrow and the terminal division Desfa- are preserved.
Joined to Desfa- above, this means the rainbow dissolving or disappearing. The continuation closes the second example under Niji.

runs.text: Feição de arco do ceo. Vt,

lines.note: Nijigata denotes a rainbow-like or arched shape. The example starts with Mado, a window, in roman type at the right end of the same row.
The example describes making a window opening in an arched shape. The Portuguese repeats that construction and divides fei-/ção across the physical rows.
This completes the phrase describing the window's rainbow or arch shape. It remains the continuation of the Nijigata example.
Nijiri describes moving while sliding or rubbing along the ground. The close-set Irſeroçando is retained without modernizing the spacing or the historical contraction pollo.
Nijiriyori adds approaching to the sliding motion of the previous entry. The Portuguese describes drawing nearer while rubbing or sliding along a surface specified below.
The surface is the ground. This short continuation completes the definition of Nijiriyori and retains pollo as printed.

runs.text: Sinal, ou diuiſa que ſe pinta ſobre

lines.note: Nijiruxi is an identifying mark or device painted on baggage. The scan supplies the t in pinta, omitted by the draft's pina; the object carrying the mark follows below.
Fato here is the baggage or load on which the identifying mark is painted. This closes the Nijiruxi entry.

Nijit means two suns. The example begins the maxim that there are not two suns in heaven. The close-set nijitnaqu is retained as in the aligned draft: its narrow internal gap does not securely establish a printed word space.

runs.text: No ceo não ha dous ſo-

lines.note: The Japanese continues with there not being two rulers on earth. The Portuguese starts with the parallel statement about heaven and divides ſo-/ẽs between rows.

runs.text: ẽs, nem na terra, ou reino dous ſenhores.

lines.note: This completes the maxim: neither two suns in heaven nor two lords in a land or kingdom. The wording is the dictionary's explanation, not a supplied expansion of the Japanese.
The entry describes twenty-eight stars or celestial signs. The mark over u is visibly downward-pointing, so Nijǔ replaces the draft's grave-marked Nijù without otherwise changing the headword.

runs.text: que os Iapoẽs, & Chinas nomeão por nomes de

lines.note: The dictionary attributes the naming of these celestial signs to Japanese and Chinese people. The printed nasal marks and historical forms Iapoẽs and Chinas are retained.
The names are those of animals, completing the dictionary's explanation of Nijǔfaxxucu. This single-word line is a body continuation, not a label or catchword.
Nimame is glossed as cooked grains or pulses. The nasal mark in Grãos belongs to the Portuguese word and has not been expanded into an extra letter.
Nimô is paraphrased by Mimiqiqu and glossed as hearing. The clearly upward-pointing mark over o is retained, along with the final S. label in the gloss's typeface.
Nimochi denotes the person who carries the baggage or load. The Portuguese is a complete single-row explanation.
Nimot names the baggage itself, contrasting with the bearer in the preceding entry. The historical final t is retained rather than expanding the word to a modern Japanese form.

Nina is glossed as snails. Enlarged reinspection shows the dotted letter after u descending below the baseline with a hook, so Caramujos replaces the draft's Caramuios on graphic evidence, not through a general modernization of consonantal i.
Nin-ai concerns human dealings and sociability. Its internal hyphen is printed within the headword, not a physical line-break sign; Vt introduces the example below.
The example describes a person good to deal with, rendered in Portuguese as gentle and of good conversation or company. The Japanese's spacing differs from the hyphenated headword and is preserved.
This completes the description of someone agreeable to converse or associate with. It is the end of the Nin-ai example rather than a separate social category.
This noun Ninai denotes buckets used for carrying water. It is distinct from the social term immediately above and is followed by the related carrying verb.
The verb describes carrying a load on the shoulders. The final s of ombros is very worn beside the right rule but has surviving ink; that chosen plural reading is a nonblocking graphic uncertainty.

runs.text: que tenha peſo diante, & de tras.

lines.note: The carried object has weight in front and behind. This qualifies the shoulder-carried load in the Ninai definition and retains the printed separation de tras.

runs.text: Andas que leuão às costas, ou aos

lines.note: Ninaigoxi is explained as a litter or carrying frame borne on the back or shoulders. The Portuguese alternative continues on the next row, and the accent in às is visible.
Shoulders completes the explanation of the carrying frame. This intact occurrence also provides a nearby comparison for the worn final word of c2-l030, without replacing that line's evidence.
Ninaua is a rope used to tie or secure baggage. Both the headword and its short definition are confined to this row.
Ninauoxi means cooking something again or more thoroughly. The Portuguese retains the historical milhor, with the things being cooked listed below.
Rice and meat are examples of foods cooked again or further. This row completes the Ninauoxi definition.

runs.text: Finta, ou impoſição que paga cada

lines.note: Ninbet denotes a levy or tax paid by each individual. The scope of each continues into peßoa on the next row.

The example describes imposing the per-person levy. The printed form is retained as Ninberuo, with an r-like letter where the headword might lead one to expect t; this possible damaged-sort or printing anomaly is not silently regularized.
The Portuguese finishes the example as imposing this levy on every person. The beta-like double-s sort in peßoa is kept as ß.
Ninbu is given with the alternative Ninſocu and means a load carrier. The abbreviated q̃ leads into a relative clause on the following physical row.
The relative clause specifies a person who carries baggage. This completes the explanation of Ninbu and Ninſocu.
Ninchi is paraphrased as human wisdom or knowledge. The source's i, introduces the Japanese explanation, while the Portuguese gives the same sense concisely.
The example concerns what neither human nor celestial knowledge can reach. Its Portuguese translation starts with Não and must be read with the continuation below.

runs.text: chegar, ou abrãger o ſaber humano, nẽ celestial.

lines.note: The translation describes something beyond the reach or compass of human and celestial understanding. The nasal abbreviations abrãger and nẽ remain unexpanded.

Ninchicu combines human beings and animals; the Japanese paraphrase names both categories. The scan supports x in chicuxǒ, not the draft's a; the short Portuguese Home is retained as printed at the right edge.
And animal completes the definition begun with Home above. This row belongs to Ninchicu, not to the next entry involving heavenly beings.

Nindẽ is paraphrased as humans and heavenly beings, translated by the dictionary as man and angel. The scan restores the damaged OCR's headword, abbreviation marks and initial H in Homẽ; Anio retains the printed consonantal i, and no final stop is supplied.
